title: Right-Facing Fist Emoji 🤜 Meaning: Starting the Fist Bump
description: The right-facing fist emoji 🤜 starts a fist bump: respect, “let’s go” or “you got this.” How it pairs with 🤛, when it means a punch, and why the order matters.
summary: 🤜 is a sideways fist with its knuckles aimed right. It usually starts a fist bump, offering respect, encouragement or thanks, and is completed by 🤛 placed after it. Without a partner it can still mean “let’s go” or “you got this,” and in jokes it sometimes stands for a punch.
meaning: Because English text runs left to right, 🤜 naturally leads. Writing it first is like extending your fist toward someone; the left-facing 🤛 then arrives to meet it. That makes 🤜 the inviting half of the pair. Sent on its own at the end of a message, it holds the fist out and waits, and a friend who replies 🤛 has completed the bump.

Its mood leans toward momentum. People use 🤜 to hype each other up before an exam, a race or a job interview: “you’re going to crush it 🤜.” The forward-driving shape feels like encouragement in motion. After the event, the full 🤜🤛 marks a shared win. Either way it is supportive and informal, closer to a teammate’s nudge than a formal congratulation.

There is a combative side too. In cartoonish banter, a right-facing fist followed by a collision symbol and a dazed face can stage a punch landing: “🤜💥😵.” Boxing and MMA fans use it when discussing a knockout. These uses depend on surrounding emojis to make the violence obvious and comic; without them, readers default to the friendly meaning.

It was added in 2016 alongside its mirrored twin, so the fist bump could finally be drawn as two people meeting rather than as a single fist aimed at the viewer. The pair is now the usual way to type the gesture. It accepts skin tones, and some friends deliberately bump fists in two different shades to represent each of them.

contexts.label: Before a big moment
contexts.body: This is where 🤜 shines on its own. A friend facing a driving test, a first day at a new job or a game-deciding free throw gets “you’ve got this 🤜.” It reads as confident backing, the gesture you would give someone on their way out the door. A returned 🤛 means they took the encouragement to heart.

contexts.label: In sports and gaming
contexts.body: Squads use 🤜🤛 to say “let’s do this” before a match and “good game” after it. In fight-sport talk, a lone fist can stand for a jab or a knockout, particularly next to 💥 or 🥊. Context makes the difference, and a teammate’s fist bump and a fight recap are rarely confused with each other.

contexts.label: Between friends
contexts.body: A fist bump is a low-key way to say thanks or seal a deal: “dinner’s on me next time 🤜.” It works well among people who find hearts too sentimental. It also patches up small disagreements, since sending 🤜 after an argument offers a no-hard-feelings truce that is easy for the other person to accept.

contexts.label: At work
contexts.body: In team chats it suits congratulations on a launch or thanks to a colleague who stayed late to help. It is casual, so it fits relaxed, friendly workplaces better than formal ones. A thumbs-up is the safer default with managers you do not know well or with partners outside the company.

Strength and encouragement: go get it.
A punch connecting, usually in fight talk or slapstick jokes.
Fired up and ready; hype before a game or challenge.

confusedWith.difference: 🤛 points left and normally answers 🤜. Each alone means the same thing; together, the right-facing fist goes first so the two meet. Sending them in the wrong order makes the fists point apart.
👊 faces the viewer head-on, so it can feel like a punch aimed at you or a bump offered straight on. 🤜 is a profile view and reads more naturally as the start of a sideways fist bump.
💪 shows a flexed arm and means strength, effort or gym progress. 🤜 is about connection and encouragement rather than personal power, though both turn up in hype messages.

avoid: Do not use it in condolences or apologies for serious hurt, where a fist bump seems flippant.
Avoid the punch meaning around real conflicts, where even cartoon violence can look threatening.
design: A clenched fist drawn in profile, knuckles aimed right, with the thumb wrapped over the curled fingers. Vendors use the same default yellow as other hand emojis and add shading or outlines in their usual style. On most platforms it is a straightforward mirror of 🤛, so the pair lines up cleanly in text. Skin tones are supported.

faqs.q: What does 🤜 mean from a girl?
faqs.a: Usually friendly support or a sign of respect, like “nice job” or “we’re good.” It is a platonic gesture, often used with friends or teammates. If she sends it before something you are nervous about, she is cheering you on.
Only the direction. 🤜 points right and is typed first; 🤛 points left and follows. In that order they look like two fists meeting in a bump. Each can also be sent alone with the same friendly meaning.

Not normally. Most people read it as a fist bump or encouragement. It becomes aggressive only with clear cues, such as explosion or injured-face emojis, angry words, or a conflict already underway. Without those, assume it is meant warmly.

faqs.q: How do you reply to a fist bump emoji?
faqs.a: Send 🤛 back to complete it, or reply with 🤜🤛 to show the full bump. A thumbs-up or a short “anytime” also works. Leaving a fist bump unanswered is not rude, but returning it is a nice touch.
